label: Thriller
description: High-stakes suspense: a ticking clock, a capable protagonist under pressure, planted twists and short, propulsive chapters.
voice: Tight third person, past tense; short chapters and short paragraphs in action.
A ticking clock is always visible: a deadline, a countdown, a hostage.
Procedure grounds it: how the lock, the gun, the database actually works.
Twists are planted early and paid off fairly.
Dialogue is clipped, subtext-heavy, often lying.
Every chapter ends on a hook or a turn.

structure.guide: A crime, an attack or a discovery that cannot be ignored.
The protagonist is pulled in personally; the clock starts.
The first lead pays off and makes things worse.
structure.then: Investigate and survive; each chapter a clue and an attack.

structure.guide: The enemy is not who they seemed, or the protagonist is now the hunted.
The clock nearly runs out; an ally dies or turns.
Face-to-face with the antagonist on their ground.
The truth out, the cost paid, one last twist.

outline_guidance: Each chapter has one clue and one threat. Keep the clock visible. Plant the twist ingredients early.
outline_example: Cold Storage | In the basement of the Harwick Clinic, Dana Ruiz finds the missing courier's phone in a freezer drawer | The call log shows her own partner phoned him an hour before he vanished | The freezer's lock clicks shut behind her
scene_guidance: Enter late, leave on a turn.
Let the reader know one thing the hero does not.
worldbuilding: The institutions involved and their rules
cliches: the ticking clock of his heart
sample:
The drawer was labelled 14 and should have held tissue samples.

It held a phone in a freezer bag, screen fogged, battery at nine percent.

Dana thumbed it awake through the plastic. Last call: 21:04. Duration: two minutes.

She knew the number. She had it saved under 'Mike'.

Behind her, the door to the cold room swung shut, and the lock made a small, polite sound.
